name: Christopher Columbus
info: Christopher Columbus (1451–1506) was a navigator from the Republic of Genoa whose four voyages for the Catholic Monarchs of Spain, from 1492, began lasting European contact with the Americas, and whose governorship of Hispaniola was marked by enslavement and brutality.

facts.born: Between 25 August and 31 October 1451 in the Republic of Genoa, by scholarly consensus; son of Domenico Colombo, a wool weaver, and Susanna Fontanarossa
facts.died: 20 May 1506 in Valladolid, aged 54, after years of illness then thought to be gout, which some modern commentators suspect was reactive arthritis
facts.role: Merchant seaman and business agent (from 1473); Admiral of the Ocean Sea, Viceroy and Governor of the lands he claimed for Castile under the Capitulations of Santa Fe (1492); removed from his posts in 1500
facts.known: the first voyage of 1492 and the landfall at Guanahani; four voyages across the Atlantic (1492–1504); naming the inhabitants indios; the encomienda and slave raids on Hispaniola; his arrest by Francisco de Bobadilla in 1500; the Columbian exchange named after him; the pleitos colombinos

t: A Genoese seaman who had traded from the British Isles to the Guinea coast, Columbus won the backing of Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492 for a westward route to Asia built on a badly underestimated size of the Earth.

His landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 and three later voyages opened the Caribbean and the coasts of South and Central America to Spain, though he never clearly renounced his belief that he had reached the Far East.

As governor of Hispaniola he waged war on the Taíno, imposed tribute and the encomienda and shipped enslaved people to Spain; accused of tyranny, he was arrested in 1500, and historians still dispute how far the depopulation that followed was his doing.
dyk: Stranded on Jamaica in 1504, Columbus kept the island's inhabitants supplying his men by predicting the lunar eclipse of 29 February, using Abraham Zacuto's astronomical charts.
ev: Born in the Republic of Genoa to Domenico Colombo, a wool weaver, and Susanna Fontanarossa
Shipwrecked off Lagos, Portugal, after his Genoese trading fleet is attacked, and settles in Lisbon
Agrees the Capitulations of Santa Fe with Ferdinand and Isabella in April, sails from Palos in August and reaches Guanahani in the Bahamas in October
Returns to a hero's welcome with captured Taínos, then leaves Cádiz with 17 ships and nearly 1,500 men to found colonies
Rounds up about 1,500 Arawaks in a slave raid on Hispaniola and ships about 500 to Spain, about two hundred of whom die on the way
On his third voyage sends boats ashore on the Paria Peninsula, the first recorded European landing on the mainland of South America
Arrested by Francisco de Bobadilla after charges of tyranny and brutality, and sent back to Spain in chains
Dies in Valladolid while still pressing the Crown for the privileges promised him in 1492

sections.early:
By scholarly consensus Christopher Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa between 25 August and 31 October 1451, though authors over the centuries have claimed him for other countries. His father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool weaver in Genoa and Savona who also kept a cheese stand where the boy worked; his mother was Susanna Fontanarossa. He had three brothers, among them Bartholomew, later a cartographer in Lisbon, and a sister. His native tongue was presumably Ligurian; in Spanish he was Cristóbal Colón. By his own account he went to sea at fourteen.

From 1473 he worked as a business agent for the Spinola, Centurione and Di Negro families, sailing to Chios and, in 1476, with a convoy to northern Europe that probably touched Bristol and Galway. Shipwrecked off Lagos that August, he settled in Lisbon, where he lived from 1477 to 1485, traded for sugar in Madeira and married Felipa Perestrello e Moniz, daughter of the donatary captain of Porto Santo. Their son Diego was born in 1479 or 1480. Between 1482 and 1485 he traded on the West African coast as far as Elmina. Largely self-educated, he learned Latin, Portuguese and Castilian and read Ptolemy, Pierre d'Ailly's Imago Mundi and Marco Polo; the historian Edmund Morgan judged that his ideas were "characteristically simple and strong and sometimes wrong".
sections.rise:
In the 1480s Columbus and his brother proposed reaching the East Indies by sailing west. His figures rested on errors: following Ptolemy and Alfraganus's Arabic miles he took the Earth to be far smaller than it is, and he put Japan about 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canary Islands, against an actual 10,600. About 1484 the advisers of John II of Portugal rejected the plan on exactly those grounds, and a second approach in 1488 failed as Bartolomeu Dias returned from rounding the southern tip of Africa.

He moved to Castile in 1485, where in 1487 he took as his mistress Beatriz Enríquez de Arana, mother of his son Fernando. He presented his plan to Queen Isabella on 1 May 1486; her committee, like the Portuguese, found the distance grossly underestimated, but the monarchs kept him on an allowance. After Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada in January 1492, a council under Hernando de Talavera again found the scheme implausible. Columbus had left for France when the king's clerk Luis de Santángel persuaded the queen, and a royal guard brought him back. The Capitulations of Santa Fe of April 1492 promised him, if he succeeded, the rank of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, the viceroyalty and governorship of any lands he claimed, and a tenth of their revenues in perpetuity.
sections.deeds:
Columbus left Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, and on 12 October landed on an island of the Bahamas its people called Guanahani. He called its inhabitants indios, wrote in his journal that they "should be good and intelligent servants", and took captives to guide him to gold. After Cuba and Hispaniola, where the Santa María ran aground and he left 39 men at La Navidad, he returned to Spain in March 1493 and presented kidnapped Taínos at court. His printed letter spread the news through Europe.

His second voyage left Cádiz in September 1493 with 17 ships and nearly 1,500 men. He found La Navidad burned and its men killed, and founded La Isabela, where disease and famine had killed two-thirds of the settlers by the end of 1494. Men he sent under Pedro Margarit raped, enslaved and robbed the islanders; Columbus then made war on the Taíno for nine months until they agreed to pay tribute, introduced the encomienda, and in February 1495 rounded up about 1,500 Arawaks, shipping about 500 to Spain as slaves. On the third voyage, in 1498, his men landed on the Paria Peninsula, the first recorded European landing on the South American mainland. The fourth, from 1502, explored the coasts of Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama in search of a strait to the Indian Ocean.
sections.opponents:
Columbus's rule on Hispaniola drew complaints from settlers as well as from the colonised. On his return in 1498 he found Spaniards in rebellion and hanged at least one leader. Accusations of tyranny and incompetence reached the court, which sent Francisco de Bobadilla to investigate. Bobadilla took depositions from the Admiral's enemies, declared himself governor and reported that Columbus governed by torture and mutilation: a man who stole corn had his ears and nose cut off and was sold into slavery, and the dismembered bodies of rebels were paraded through the streets. Columbus denied the charges, and historians have disputed the report's neutrality, given the Spaniards' anti-Italian sentiment and Bobadilla's wish for his post. In October 1500 he was sent to Spain in chains.

Later judgements divide sharply. The Spanish historian Consuelo Varela wrote that his government "was characterized by a form of tyranny"; Basil Davidson called him the "father of the slave trade"; George Tinker and Mark Freedman argue that he began a cycle of "murder, violence, and slavery" that disease alone cannot explain. Kris Lane disputes the word genocide where the atrocities were not intended, William J. Connell warns against judging the 15th century by 20th-century morality, and others hold that some accounts were exaggerated as part of the Black Legend. A study of Spanish archives found that the gold quotas were imposed by the cacique Guarionex, and no record of hands cut off for failing to pay them.
sections.last:
Ferdinand ordered Columbus released after six weeks in jail; the monarchs restored his freedom and wealth and agreed to fund a fourth voyage, but named Nicolás de Ovando governor of the Indies in his place. On that voyage, in 1502, he was refused entry to Santo Domingo with a hurricane approaching; his own ships survived while 20 of the 30 ships of the outgoing treasure fleet were lost with 500 lives. In June 1503 his damaged ships were beached on Jamaica, where he and 230 men were stranded for a year while Ovando, who detested him, obstructed their rescue. He reached Sanlúcar on 7 November 1504.

He grew increasingly religious and, probably with his son Diego and the Carthusian monk Gaspar Gorricio, compiled a Book of Privileges (1502) setting out what the Crown owed him and a Book of Prophecies (1505) placing his voyages within Christian eschatology. Ill since his first return voyage with attacks then taken for gout, sometimes bedridden for months, he settled in Seville in 1505 and followed the court to Segovia and Valladolid to press his claim to a tenth of the riches of the new lands. The Crown, holding that his removal as governor released it from the contract, refused. He died in Valladolid on 20 May 1506, aged 54. His heirs pursued the claims in the pleitos colombinos, which ran in various forms until 1790.
sections.legacy:
Columbus's voyages are considered a turning point in human history and often cited as the beginning of the modern era. They brought lasting contact between the hemispheres; the indigenous cultures before them are called pre-Columbian, and the movement of people, plants, animals, diseases and ideas that followed is known as the Columbian exchange. Exposed to Old World diseases, warfare and forced labour, the peoples of the Caribbean collapsed: within three to six decades the surviving Arawaks numbered in the hundreds. Scholars weigh the causes differently, Noble David Cook stressing smallpox and Andrés Reséndez slavery in the mines, and Samuel Eliot Morison, his biographer, wrote that the policy Columbus began "resulted in complete genocide".

For a century after his death his reputation suffered from his failures as an administrator. After the American Revolution he became a founding figure for the United States, lending his name to Columbia, and later an ethnic hero for Italian, Irish and Jewish immigrants; the 1893 Chicago fair was named the World's Columbian Exposition, and Spain made 12 October its national day. From the 1990s a narrative of genocide and destruction came to compete with that of the heroic discoverer. Edmundo O'Gorman rejected the idea that he "discovered" America as a later legend, the Norse had reached North America about 500 years earlier, and after 2020 many of his monuments were removed.

summary: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator in Spanish service, crossed the Atlantic four times between 1492 and 1504 and began the European colonisation of the Americas, while maintaining that he had reached Asia. His governorship of Hispaniola, with its wars, tribute and slave raids, ended in his arrest in 1500, and his place in history has moved from heroic discoverer to a figure of sharp dispute.

notes: Birth: the article gives 'between 25 August and 31 October 1451' and calls Genoa the scholarly consensus; other origin theories mentioned only in passing.

The article's fourth-voyage paragraph calls Francisco de Bobadilla 'the new governor' who refused Columbus port at Santo Domingo, while the previous paragraph says Ovando replaced Bobadilla, and Bobadilla died in the fleet; I left out who refused him and said only that he was refused entry and that the outgoing fleet was lost.
The 1492 'Bulls of Donation' and Treaty of Tordesillas left out for length.
The hand-cutting for gold quotas is told as disputed, as the article gives it (Las Casas's account against an archival study).

Population figures for pre-Columbian Hispaniola (250,000 to two million, or 10,000–50,000 from 2020 genetic analysis) left out of the text for length; the 'hundreds within three to six decades' figure kept.
Remains: the Seville/Santo Domingo dispute left out.
